object_types.name: Vendor
object_types.definition: A supplier from which the business can purchase goods or services, identified by a vendor number generated at record creation.

source_references.excerpt: The vendor record. It's the thing in the supplier master.

object_types.name: SpendTier
object_types.definition: Classification of a vendor based on spending volume and relationship value.

source_references.excerpt: Every vendor has a tier. Bronze, silver, gold.
I'm talking about spend. Gold vendors are the ones we spend real money with, they get quarterly business reviews, better payment terms, a named relationship manager.

object_types.name: RiskTier
object_types.definition: Classification of a vendor based on compliance risk derived from the risk review.

source_references.excerpt: I use low, medium, high.
And I'm talking about risk. Low, medium, high, based on the review -- what data they touch, what geography they operate in, whether they're a sole source.

source_references.excerpt: The review is its own record. It has a review ID, because we need to know who signed it and when, and auditors ask. It's not a checkbox on the vendor.

ambiguities.description: Vendor address specification: Three types of addresses are mentioned (remit-to, ship-from, legal), but the model for how they are stored is unclear. Are they separate attributes on the Vendor entity, a single composite address, or a repeating structure? The model currently omits address entirely because the details are unspecified.

source_references.excerpt: Address, though we have three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one, which are frequently different and frequently wrong.

ambiguities.description: Risk Review lifecycle and optionality: The rule is clear that active vendors must have a current signed-off review, but draft vendors start with no review. The model captures that reviews accumulate over time and one is marked current. However, the mechanism for determining 'current' is not explicit (timestamp-based, system flag, etc.), and whether a suspended vendor retains or loses its current review status is unclear.

source_references.excerpt: A vendor can have several reviews over its life -- we re-review on a cycle, and every re-review is a new record, we don't edit the old one. But one of them is the current one... A vendor accumulates review records over time. At most one is the current one. Being active requires a current signed-off review.

ambiguities.description: Purchase Order and Vendor Status transition control: The transcript establishes that POs cannot be raised against inactive vendors (enforced at creation), but the rule for what happens to in-flight POs when a vendor transitions to suspended is explicitly unresolved. The statement 'what happens to in-flight purchase orders when a vendor is suspended is undecided' captures an incomplete business rule. A future model iteration must address whether POs block suspension, remain linked without processing, or are automatically cancelled.

source_references.excerpt: That's the control at creation. What we have never settled is what happens after... If we suspend a vendor -- their review lapses, or there's a breach, or they turn up on a sanctions list -- what happens to the purchase orders already in flight?... Parking it explicitly: what happens to in-flight purchase orders when a vendor is suspended is undecided.

ambiguities.description: Spend Tier vs. Risk Tier naming collision: Stakeholders use the term 'tier' for two independent attributes with different semantics (spending volume vs. compliance risk). While the model correctly separates them into SpendTier and RiskTier, the business process still conflates the terms verbally ('high tier vendor'), creating ongoing operational confusion acknowledged as 'a genuine chaos' and 'a losing battle for two years.' The model has resolved the technical issue but not the organizational one.

source_references.excerpt: Let's do tier. Mei, in the system, are those the same field? No. Two separate fields, different values, different owners. Procurement sets one, compliance sets the other... Someone says 'that's a high tier vendor' in a meeting and half the room hears 'big spender' and the other half hears 'dangerous,'... Can a vendor be gold and high at the same time? Most of our cloud providers are exactly that. Big spend, high risk.

ambiguities.description: VendorContact to Vendor relationship cardinality: The model captures that a vendor may operate in zero, one, or multiple regions, and each region gets exactly one contact. However, the bidirectional question -- can multiple vendors use the same contact person (same email/name) in the same region -- is not addressed. The fact type 'VendorContact is for Vendor in Region' implies one contact per vendor-region pair, but does not indicate whether the same ContactId can appear in multiple such tuples.

source_references.excerpt: Each vendor has one primary contact... Since we went to regional sourcing last year, it's one primary contact per region... If they don't operate in that region, there's nothing there at all. Most of our vendors are one region only. It's the big ones that are multi-region.

ambiguities.description: Purchase order state and fulfillment tracking: The model captures PO number, amount, raised date, and vendor, but no other state information (e.g., fulfilled, partial, pending delivery, received). The transcript mentions 'goods on a ship' and receiving workflow, but these details fall outside the stated scope. It is unclear whether the model should eventually track PO status, delivery status, or receipt status, or whether those belong in a separate order-fulfillment domain.

source_references.excerpt: There's a lot -- line items, delivery dates, cost centre, approvals. But if we go there we'll be here all day and I don't think that's what you're after today... I'll take vendor, number, amount, date and we can extend later.
We have purchase orders where the goods are physically on a ship.

ambiguities.description: Tax ID uniqueness and duplicate vendors: While the model correctly identifies VendorNumber as the unique identifier and notes that TaxId is not unique, the scope of the duplicate-vendor problem and whether a 'merge' or 'link' operation exists to handle it is unknown. The transcript mentions 'a cleanup project that's been on the roadmap for two years,' indicating this is a known data quality issue but not a modeled business rule.

source_references.excerpt: Could you identify a vendor by tax ID instead? You'd think so, but no. We have vendors with the same tax ID -- different legal entities under one parent that file together, or we've onboarded the same company twice by accident and nobody's merged them... The duplicates are a real problem. There's a cleanup project that's been on the roadmap for two years.

ambiguities.description: Region set completeness and future expansion: Four regions are currently defined (EMEA, APAC, NA, LATAM), but the transcript indicates discussion of potentially splitting EMEA in the future. The model captures the current four-value constraint but does not account for whether regions can be dynamically added or whether the set is fixed by design. This affects system flexibility.

source_references.excerpt: Region code. EMEA, APAC, NA, LATAM. Four regions, fixed? Four today. There's been talk of splitting EMEA but it hasn't happened.

ambiguities.description: Vendor Contact information completeness: The model captures ContactName, ContactEmail, and ContactPhoneNumber as attributes of VendorContact, but the transcript does not clarify whether all three are mandatory or optional, or whether additional contact attributes (title, department, physical address) should be included. The phrase 'Name, email, phone number' is descriptive but does not state optionality.

source_references.excerpt: Each vendor has one primary contact. Name, email, phone number.

ambiguities.description: Vendor status transition rules: The model captures the three valid status values (draft, active, suspended) and the mandatory-to-active constraint via risk review completion. However, the complete state machine (e.g., can a vendor go from suspended back to active? can draft skip to suspended? are there re-onboarding flows?) is not discussed, leaving transition rules incomplete.

source_references.excerpt: What are the statuses? Draft, active, suspended... A vendor cannot be moved to active until a risk review has been completed and signed off.

ambiguities.description: Preferred vendor column in spreadsheet: The transcript mentions a 'preferred' flag in Mei's informal spreadsheet indicating when one vendor should be chosen over another if multiple suppliers are available. This is noted as ad hoc with no defined criteria ('genuinely ad hoc, don't model it'). However, the business impact suggests this could evolve into a formal business rule. The model correctly excludes it as non-formalized, but this is a gap to revisit.

source_references.excerpt: There's a column called 'preferred.' It means if two vendors can supply the same thing, buy from this one... Who decides preferred? Officially nobody... If you tell me the criteria, I'll model it. If it's genuinely ad hoc, modeling it would be inventing something... It's ad hoc. Don't model it.
